sweep_summary: Estonian (esto1258), catalog kind weight-hedged on Asu & Teras 2009 JIPA. Of the 11 sweep items, 3 are not about Estonian (Wightman 1992, Turk 1992, Turk et al. 2006), 3 are sentence-prosody or quantity works (Sahkai & Tamm 2018/2019, Lehiste 2012), and 5 bear on word prosody: Eek 1990 (Linguistica Uralica, CC-BY, fetched sources and read: foot-based account with main stress on the most prominent first foot, rhythmic secondary stress, morphemic suffix stress, no adjacent stresses - refines), Prince 1980 (LI, JSTOR-paywalled, no open copy - high priority, the metrical source behind the weight wording), Eek 1987 (De Gruyter paywalled, stress-perception experiment - medium), Eek et al. 1997 and Lehiste 1997 (Tallinn 1997 symposium volume, print-only per ESTER, ISBN 9985851471 - low/medium). Sahkai & Tamm 2019 was fetched sources (Wayback copy of the CC-BY PDF) and is silent on word stress. Two authoritative first-hand Estonian-language statements already on file from the 9/16 fetch were read: Asu, Lippus, Pajusalu & Teras 2016 (EKH sec. 4.2, p. 127) confirms initial primary stress with rhythmic odd-syllable secondary stress subject to morphology; Eesti grammatika 2023 (FO 34-36, pp. 71-73) states the rule most explicitly, including the Q3 (overlong) condition for stress on the second syllable and secondary stress on heavy final syllables, and is proposed as the new deciding source (refines, consistent with weight-hedged). searches were done through Crossref, Semantic Scholar, Unpaywall, Europe PMC, Glottolog, ESTER and direct fetches.

new_statements.translation: FO 34. [...] Estonian is a fixed-stress language in which primary stress is on the first syllable. In interjections and loanwords, and with some derivational suffixes (e.g. -nna), a syllable other than the first may carry primary stress [...] FO 35. [...] In Estonian the odd-numbered syllables are normally stressed: the 1st syllable carries primary stress and the following odd-numbered syllables, i.e. the 3rd, 5th, 7th etc., carry secondary stress. Even-numbered syllables are unstressed. [...] A secondary-stressed syllable can immediately follow the primary-stressed syllable only in a third-quantity (Q3) word.
new_statements.citation: Metslang, Helle et al. (incl. Pire Teras, Eva Liina Asu, Pärtel Lippus, Karl Pajusalu). 2023. Eesti grammatika. Tartu: Tartu Ülikooli Kirjastus. Part I Foneetika ja fonoloogia, FO 34-36 'Sõnarõhk ja rütm', pp. 71-73. hdl:10062/94933
new_statements.reading: Primary stress fixed on the initial syllable (lexical exceptions: interjections, recent loans, suffix -nna). Secondary stress is basically rhythmic, on odd-numbered syllables (syllabic trochees), but (i) an overlong (Q3) initial syllable licenses secondary stress on the immediately following syllable (ohtlik, armsalt, aastaid), (ii) a word-final syllable closed by a long plosive or a cluster takes secondary stress (raamatut, raamatust), and (iii) suffixes like -lik, -stik, -mine attract secondary stress inconsistently; final secondary stresses can be lost in spontaneous speech. This is exactly the 'weight-hedged' picture: initial primary stress, secondary stress rhythmic with weight (Q3 / heavy final) and morphological interference. Asu et al. 2016 (EKH, sec. 4.2 p. 127) says the same in slightly less detail, and Eek 1990 (LU 26: 258-259, fetched sources open) gives the foot-based phonetic version with morphemic suffix stress and avoidance of adjacent stresses.

sources.citation: Eek, Arvo. 1990. Units of temporal organisation and word accents in Estonian. Linguistica Uralica 26(4): 251-263.
sources.quote: A word becomes a coherent whole due to the most prominent foot that carries the main stress marked by the peak of the fundamental frequency. […] The intra-foot rhythm is noticeable in a two or three-syllable foot (kava 12; kavala 132, see Fig. 6). The same tendency can be observed in a word of several feet (kava/lama 12; kava/lama/legi 132). The general scheme is violated only by those suffixes that carry morphemic stress (föö/lise/legi 123). However, there is a strong tendency to avoid two neighbouring stressed syllables (téoli/selegi 12; Fig. 6).

sources.note: Foot-based account: the word is organised into feet of 1-3 syllables, the first (most prominent) foot carries main stress (F0 peak); intra-word feet are trochaic with rhythmic weakening (kava/lama/legi 132), secondary stress on the fourth syllable (-matt-, Fig. 5b); some suffixes carry 'morphemic stress' and override the rhythm, but adjacent stressed syllables are avoided.
